svg.title: Two columns, conventional software and agentic software, aligned row for row to compare how attacker-controlled input reaches a consequential operation through a component that interprets it
svg.desc: Two columns are aligned against three numbered rows named down the left edge: row one, untrusted input; row two, the component that interprets it; row three, the consequential operation. The left column is headed CONVENTIONAL SOFTWARE, a logging framework. Its row-one box, drawn in the hostile color, reads attacker-controlled text, a user-supplied field that the application logs. A downward arrow reaches its row-two box, LOGGING FRAMEWORK, which interprets lookup syntax inside the message it was asked only to record. A second downward arrow reaches its row-three box, drawn in the hostile color, EXTERNAL OPERATION: the lookup resolves and fetches a remote resource. The right column is headed AGENTIC SOFTWARE, an agent with tool access. Its row-one box, also in the hostile color, reads attacker-controlled document, content the agent retrieves from a source it does not control. A downward arrow reaches its row-two box, AGENT CONTEXT, which treats the retrieved text as instructions rather than as data. A second downward arrow reaches its row-three box, in the hostile color, PRIVILEGED TOOL CALL: the agent acts with the permissions its tools carry. A single heavy dashed red trust boundary runs horizontally across both columns between row two and row three, labeled the boundary the engineer must enforce: which information may influence a consequential operation. Below the columns, two lists of controls sit side by side. For conventional software: remove the interpretation behavior, restrict outbound connections, and limit process privilege. For agentic software: restrict tool permissions, authorize consequential operations independently, and separate retrieved content from the instructions that govern the agent. Two closing notes read that the mechanisms differ while both raise the same question about authority across a trust boundary, and that instructions asking an agent to ignore malicious content are guidance rather than enforcement at the boundary.
svg.text: TWO WAYS UNTRUSTED INFORMATION ACQUIRES AUTHORITY
a user-supplied field the application logs
content retrieved from a source we do not control
interprets lookup syntax inside the message
the lookup resolves and fetches a remote resource
the agent acts with the permissions its tools carry
which information may influence a consequential operation, and where is that restriction applied?

g.text: Separate retrieved content from governing instructions.
The mechanisms differ. Both ask the same question about authority across a trust boundary.
Instructions asking an agent to ignore malicious content are guidance.
They are not enforcement at the boundary.
